title: South, East, and Southeast Asia, 300 BCE–1980 CE

guide.summary: This content area covers Buddhist, Hindu, Confucian, Daoist, and Islamic traditions across South, East, and Southeast Asia. Many works are sacred spaces designed for movement and ritual, cosmological diagrams in architecture, or paintings and prints shaped by court, scholarly, and urban audiences. Trade and exchange, from porcelain to Prussian blue pigment, recur throughout.

sections.heading: Buddhist and Hindu sacred spaces
sections.body:
The **Great Stupa at Sanchi** (India, begun under Ashoka) is a hemispherical mound containing relics. Pilgrims **circumambulate** it clockwise, entering through carved gateways (**toranas**).

**Borobudur** (Java, c. 800) is a vast Buddhist monument built as a stepped mountain. Pilgrims ascend through galleries of narrative reliefs toward open terraces with stupas, a journey from the world of desire toward enlightenment.

Hindu temples model the cosmic mountain. The **Lakshmana Temple** at Khajuraho (Nagara style) rises in clustered towers (**shikharas**) above the **garbhagriha**, the dark "womb chamber" holding the deity's image. **Angkor Wat** (Cambodia, twelfth century), dedicated to Vishnu, represents Mount Meru with five towers and unusually faces west, possibly connected to its funerary role.

The bronze **Shiva as Lord of Dance (Nataraja)** depicts the god dancing within a ring of fire, creating and destroying the universe, his foot on a dwarf symbolizing ignorance.

sections.heading: China and Korea
sections.body:
The **Terra cotta warriors** of Qin Shi Huangdi's tomb (c. 210 BCE), thousands of individualized soldiers, guarded the first emperor in the afterlife. The Han **Funeral banner of Lady Dai** shows three realms (heaven, earth, underworld) to guide her soul.

Fan Kuan's **Travelers among Mountains and Streams** (Northern Song, c. 1000) dwarfs tiny travelers beneath a towering mountain, reflecting a cosmic order. The Yuan dynasty **David Vases** (1351) are early dated blue-and-white porcelain, using cobalt imported from Persia, with inscriptions dedicating them to a Daoist temple.

The **Forbidden City** in Beijing embodies imperial order through axial, symmetrical planning. **Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan** (1967), a propaganda oil painting reproduced in hundreds of millions of copies during the Cultural Revolution, cast Mao as a youthful revolutionary leader.

sections.heading: Japan
sections.body:
**Todai-ji** houses a colossal bronze Buddha. **Ryoan-ji**'s dry garden (karesansui) of raked gravel and fifteen stones invites Zen meditation; from no point can all stones be seen at once. Ogata Korin's **White and Red Plum Blossoms** uses gold leaf and a stylized stream on a pair of folding screens.

Hokusai's **Under the Wave off Kanagawa** (c. 1830), a **ukiyo-e** woodblock print, frames Mount Fuji beneath a towering wave. Its imported Prussian blue pigment and its influence on European artists show global exchange.

sections.heading: Mughal India
sections.body: Mughal court painting blended Persian, Indian, and European elements. **Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings** shows the emperor on an hourglass throne, haloed, handing a book to a Sufi sage while ignoring an Ottoman sultan and King James I of England, asserting spiritual over worldly power. The **Taj Mahal**, built by Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, stands at the end of a symmetrical garden symbolizing paradise.

keyTakeaways: Buddhist and Hindu monuments model cosmic mountains and guide ritual movement.
Chinese funerary art served the afterlife of rulers and elites.
Landscape painting expressed philosophical order (Fan Kuan).
Japanese Zen gardens and ukiyo-e prints served contemplation and urban markets.
Mughal art blended traditions to assert imperial and spiritual authority.
Trade materials (cobalt, Prussian blue) connected Asia to the wider world.
commonMistakes: Confusing stupas (Buddhist relic mounds) with Hindu temples.
Forgetting that pilgrims move through Sanchi and Borobudur.
Assuming all Asian art is religious; much served courts and markets.
Mixing up Angkor Wat (Hindu, later Buddhist) and Borobudur (Buddhist).
Treating the Great Wave as a painting rather than a woodblock print.
Missing European figures in Mughal painting.
examTips: Describe how viewers moved through or used each space.
Name religious concepts precisely: circumambulation, garbhagriha, Mount Meru, enlightenment.
Global-exchange evidence (David Vases, Great Wave, Jahangir) is useful for essays on cross-cultural contact.
Know dynasties: Qin, Han, Song, Yuan, Ming/Qing; Mughal; Khmer.
Propaganda works (Chairman Mao) pair well with other political art in comparisons.
guide.cramSheet:
**South Asia:** Great Stupa Sanchi (circumambulation, toranas) · Lakshmana Temple (shikhara, garbhagriha) · Shiva Nataraja · Jahangir and Sufi shaikh · Taj Mahal

**Southeast Asia:** Borobudur (Buddhist, ascent) · Angkor Wat (Vishnu, Meru, faces west)

**China:** Terra cotta warriors (Qin) · Lady Dai banner (Han) · Fan Kuan (Song) · David Vases (Yuan, cobalt) · Forbidden City · Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan

**Japan:** Todai-ji · Ryoan-ji (Zen dry garden) · Korin plum blossoms · Hokusai Great Wave (ukiyo-e, Prussian blue)

practice.stimulus: A white marble tomb with a central onion dome and four minarets stands at the end of a long, symmetrical garden divided by water channels, built in the seventeenth century by an emperor for his wife.
practice.explanation: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal for Mumtaz Mahal; the garden evokes paradise.

distractors.C: Angkor Wat is a Khmer temple.

practice.stimulus: A towering wave with claw-like foam curls over three boats, while Mount Fuji appears small in the distance. The work was printed in many copies around 1830.
practice.stem: The work's medium and genre are

choices.text: woodblock print in the ukiyo-e tradition
oil painting in the Impressionist tradition

practice.explanation: Hokusai's Under the Wave off Kanagawa was produced as a woodblock print for a broad urban market.

distractors.B: It influenced Impressionists but is a Japanese print.

practice.stimulus: Thousands of life-size ceramic soldiers, each with individualized features, were buried in pits near the tomb of China's first emperor around 210 BCE.

choices.text: protect and serve the emperor in the afterlife
be displayed in a public museum

practice.explanation: The Terra cotta warriors of Qin Shi Huangdi formed an army for the afterlife.

practice.stimulus: A bronze statue shows a four-armed god dancing within a ring of flames. One foot rests on a small figure; one hand holds a drum and another holds fire.

choices.text: Shiva as Lord of Dance, creating and destroying the universe

practice.explanation: The drum signals creation, the fire destruction, and the figure underfoot ignorance.

distractors.B: The Buddha is shown seated in meditation, not dancing.

practice.stimulus: A hemispherical mound in India containing relics is surrounded by a stone railing and four elaborately carved gateways. Worshippers walk clockwise around it.
practice.stem: Walking around the monument is significant because

choices.text: circumambulation is a devotional act that aligns the worshipper with the cosmic order and the Buddha's teachings
it was the only way to reach the interior altar
it measured the size of the building
it was required to pay a toll

practice.explanation: At the Great Stupa at Sanchi, the solid mound has no interior space; devotion happens through movement around it.

practice.stimulus: A twelfth-century temple in Cambodia, dedicated to Vishnu, has five lotus-shaped towers rising above concentric galleries and is surrounded by a wide moat. Unusually, it faces west.
practice.stem: The temple's layout most likely symbolizes

choices.text: Mount Meru, the center of the universe, surrounded by mountains and oceans

practice.explanation: Angkor Wat's towers represent Meru's peaks, its walls the mountains, and the moat the cosmic ocean; its western orientation may relate to its funerary role.

practice.stimulus: A ninth-century monument in Java is built as a stepped pyramid. Lower galleries are lined with narrative reliefs; the upper terraces are open, circular, and lined with bell-shaped stupas containing Buddha statues.
practice.stem: The monument's design most likely represents

choices.text: a path from the world of desire toward enlightenment as pilgrims ascend
the tomb of a Mughal emperor

practice.explanation: Borobudur moves from enclosed narrative galleries to open, abstract terraces, mirroring a spiritual ascent.

practice.stimulus: A tall hanging scroll shows a massive mountain filling the upper composition, with a thin waterfall. At the bottom, tiny figures lead mules along a path.
practice.stem: The scale of the travelers relative to the mountain most likely suggests

choices.text: humanity's small place within a vast natural and cosmic order
that the travelers are far from home

practice.explanation: Fan Kuan's Travelers among Mountains and Streams reflects Neo-Confucian and Daoist ideas about harmony and hierarchy in nature.

practice.stimulus: At a Zen temple in Kyoto, a rectangular garden of raked white gravel holds fifteen stones in small groups. Visitors sit on a veranda to view it. From any single point, at least one stone is hidden.
practice.stem: The garden is designed primarily for
practice.explanation: Ryoan-ji's spare dry garden encourages stillness and reflection; the hidden stone resists complete understanding.

distractors.C: Visitors view it from a veranda, not walking through it.

practice.stimulus: A seventeenth-century Mughal painting shows the emperor, with a large halo, seated on an hourglass throne, handing a book to an elderly Sufi sage. An Ottoman sultan and the English king James I stand below, along with the artist himself.
practice.stem: The painting's central message is that the emperor

choices.text: values spiritual wisdom above worldly power and diplomacy
is subordinate to the English king

practice.explanation: Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings uses the halo and the act of preference to elevate the emperor's spiritual status.

distractors.B: James I is shown below and ignored.

practice.stimulus: A 1967 oil painting shows a young Mao Zedong in a scholar's robe striding across hills with an umbrella, clouds parting behind him. Hundreds of millions of reproductions circulated during the Cultural Revolution.
practice.stem: The painting's function is best described as

choices.text: political propaganda building a heroic cult of personality around Mao
a private landscape painting for scholars
a religious icon for a Buddhist temple

practice.explanation: Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan used Western realist oil technique and mass reproduction to create an idealized revolutionary image.

practice.stimulus: A T-shaped painted silk banner from a Han dynasty tomb shows, from top to bottom, celestial beings and the sun and moon; an elderly woman with attendants; a funeral offering; and underworld creatures.
practice.stem: The banner's structure most likely served to

choices.text: map the realms of heaven, earth, and the underworld to guide the deceased's soul
decorate a palace hall for banquets

practice.explanation: The Funeral banner of Lady Dai places her within a cosmological framework for the afterlife.

distractors.C: It predates Buddhism's spread in China.

practice.stimulus: At a temple in Khajuraho, a cluster of towers rises progressively higher toward the tallest one above the inner sanctum. The sanctum is small and dark and holds the deity's image.
practice.stem: How does the temple's design express Hindu concepts?

choices.text: The towers evoke a cosmic mountain, and the dark garbhagriha suggests a sacred womb where the devotee encounters the deity.
The bright, open sanctum welcomes large congregations for sermons.
The design imitates a Roman basilica.
The towers are watchtowers for defense.

practice.explanation: The Lakshmana Temple's Nagara design emphasizes vertical ascent and an intimate, dark core for darshan (seeing the deity).

distractors.B: The sanctum is small and dark.

practice.stimulus: A pair of tall porcelain vases with cobalt blue dragons is dated 1351 by an inscription dedicating them, with an incense burner, to a Daoist temple. The cobalt was imported from Persia.
practice.stem: The vases are significant to art historians primarily because they

choices.text: are among the earliest dated blue-and-white porcelains and reflect trade networks across the Mongol empire
were used as funerary urns for emperors

practice.explanation: The David Vases anchor the chronology of blue-and-white ware; Persian cobalt shows Yuan-era exchange.

distractors.C: The inscription dedicates them to a temple.

practice.stimulus: The work is Under the Wave off Kanagawa (also called The Great Wave), from the series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji by Katsushika Hokusai, c. 1830–1833, polychrome woodblock print.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how Hokusai uses composition to create drama.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe TWO visual elements that show the influence of artistic exchange between Japan and the wider world.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how the woodblock medium affected the work's audience.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain the significance of including Mount Fuji in the composition.

rubric.description: The huge wave arcs across the composition and dwarfs the boats, framing a tiny Mount Fuji; the wave's claw-like crest is poised to crash.
Use of imported Prussian blue pigment.
A low horizon and Western-influenced perspective with the distant mountain small, reflecting contact with European prints.
Woodblock printing allowed many inexpensive copies, so the image reached a broad urban audience (and later, European collectors).
Fuji was a sacred symbol of Japan and associated with immortality; showing it calm and enduring behind the threatening wave contrasts permanence with human vulnerability.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Hokusai fills most of the composition with a gigantic wave that curves over three boats, its crest breaking into claw-like fingers of foam. The boatmen crouch beneath it, and Mount Fuji appears tiny in the gap below the wave, so the viewer feels the wave is about to crash.

(b) Hokusai used Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment imported from Europe, which gives the waves their intense color. He also used a low horizon and a Western-style sense of perspective, with Fuji small in the distance, reflecting knowledge of European prints that reached Japan through Dutch trade.

(c) Because woodblocks could print many copies cheaply, the work was affordable for ordinary townspeople, not just elites. Later, prints like this reached Europe, where they influenced Impressionist artists.

(d) Mount Fuji was a sacred mountain and national symbol associated with immortality. Placing it calm and stable behind the violent wave contrasts the fragility of human life with Fuji's endurance, which suited the series' focus on Fuji.
